articles.title: Democratic socialist defeats incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayor's race
articles.summary: The results mean America's two most populous cities - New York and Los Angeles - will be led by democratic socialists.

blocks.text: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.

Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office.
Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms.

Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.

Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken."

"Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

items: Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch
Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?
'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat

blocks.text: Raman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again".

She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city.

The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster.
The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.

articles.title: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
articles.summary: The Delhi government has announced a four-month winter action plan, but experts say that won't be enough.

blocks.text: There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.

Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?

This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.

Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.

This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.

For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.

The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.

Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.

Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.

"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.

"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."

Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.

"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."

Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.

items: 'I panic every time she coughs' - Delhi's toxic air is making its children sick
Why India caps pollution reading at 500 when the air is far more toxic
Can artificial rain fix toxic air in India's capital?
Living in Delhi smog is like watching a dystopian film again and again

blocks.text: In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".

On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.

The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".
Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.
A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.
For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.

Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.
While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.
Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.
Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.
The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.
"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.
"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

articles.title: FACT CHECK: ICC’s arrest warrant vs Dela Rosa still active, not dismissed by SC
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court's arrest warrant against Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa remains in effect. Nor has the Philippine Supreme Court dismissed proceedings against him.

blocks.text: Claim: The International Criminal Court (ICC) allegedly declared its arrest warrant against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa invalid, while the Supreme Court (SC) dismissed the case and arrest warrant against him.
Why we fact-checked this: The claim originated from YouTube videos uploaded by the channel “NEWS UPDATE FILES,” which had over 80,000 subscribers, on November 1 and 2.
The video titles and thumbnails claim that the ICC had withdrawn its charges and that the SC officially dismissed the case against Dela Rosa.

As of writing, both videos reached 43,800, with over 2,000 likes in total. The comments section saw users commending the SC for the supposed dismissal and criticizing the Marcos administration’s alleged political motives.

The facts: There is no official statement, court order, or legal resolution from the ICC that invalidates the arrest warrant. It remains active and is publicly accessible in the ICC’s official records.

The tribunal unsealed and publicly confirmed the arrest warrant in May 2026. Based on the warrant, the Pre-Trial Chamber I found reasonable grounds to believe that Dela Rosa — in his former capacity as Philippine National Police chief — committed the crime against humanity of murder. This is in connection with the war on drugs campaign of former president Rodrigo Duterte, who is detained at the ICC.

Furthermore, the SC did not dismiss any ICC warrant and nor did it void the international proceedings. In fact, the former PNP chief’s legal camp continues to seek domestic remedies before the High Court, including an October 27 manifestation for reconsideration of the ruling that denied his plea for a temporary restraining order and a status quo ante order.Dela Rosa also asked the SC to block his warrant in November 2025.

As of writing, Dela Rosa remains at large, with the interior department offering a P50-million reward for information leading to his arrest.Lack of evidence: The video presents no official court orders, case numbers, or transcripts to prove its claims. Instead, it features an unidentified commentator reacting to unrelated, recycled clips of government officials, including former chief presidential legal counsel Salvador Panelo and Vice President Sara Duterte.
Debunked: Dela Rosa has been the target of false claims surrounding his ICC arrest warrant:

FACT CHECK: ‘Shoot-to-kill’ Bato dela Rosa warning by Lordan Suan is fake
FACT CHECK: No basis for claim that Bato Dela Rosa is under Trump’s protection

blocks.text: – Lyndee Buenagua/Rappler.com

articles.title: Powerhouse Parramatta opens this weekend – and it’s dazzling inside and out
articles.summary: Coups de théâtre abound in the $915m addition to western Sydney’s skyline, which opens on Saturday with five new exhibitions – and a 23-day festival

blocks.text: Dubbed the “Opera House of western Sydney”, Powerhouse Parramatta’s white lattice exoskeleton, composed from 1,300 individual pieces and wrapping 30,000 sq metres of interior space, has already become a familiar landmark.

Even better known, perhaps, is the project’s controversial history. Since the Parramatta outpost was announced in 2014, a vocal group of dissenters led by former staff and trustees has lamented what they see as the neglect of the museum’s Ultimo site in favour of a new infrastructure project, and what they say is a shift away from the museum’s core business towards contemporary art and events.

The eye-watering price tag – $915m, in an era of funding precarity for the arts – has also come under scrutiny, culminating in a New South Wales Treasury investigation into allegations over the museum’s governance and procurement practices. In late August, 10 weeks from the scheduled opening, CEO Lisa Havilah was stood down while the investigation unfolded.

blocks.caption: Task Eternal is the Powerhouse Parramatta’s flagship opening exhibition – a celebration of flight and space travel. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: When the major new venue opens to the public on Saturday, the big question will be: was it worth it? What will it bring to Parramatta – and will it be enough to bring the rest of Sydney, and the rest of Australia, out west?

Powerhouse is sweetening the pot with a 23-day opening festival of performances, parties, talks, screenings and workshops, with 65% of the program free. When Guardian Australia visited last week, the space was crowded with installation crew in hi-vis, hard hats and steel-capped boots. But even with its exhibitions in various states of readiness, it was hard not to be dazzled.
Dizzying spectacles and a sense of calm

The steel exoskeleton that has been such a prominent addition to Parramatta’s skyline is more than decorative. Encasing two towers, and built from 12,000 tonnes of steel, it’s what allows the building to boast massive column-free exhibition spaces up to 18m in height, including the largest in Australia.

But at first encounter, perhaps the most striking thing about the Moreau Kusunoki and Genton-designed building is the sense of calm it evokes. This is a building that is constantly calling you to slow down, take a breath and look beyond its architecture to the city, landscape and Parramatta River below.

blocks.caption: ‘This is a building that is constantly calling you to slow down, take a breath and look beyond.’ Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The glass facade and abundance of natural light is complemented by an airy colour palette, all creams, white and light greys – including interior walls covered in a pale, textured render made from 600,000 crushed oyster shells, locally and sustainably sourced. Wide corridors flanking the exhibition spaces are lined with chairs and lounges that invite you to pause and take in the view.

This peace is particularly necessary given the dizzying spectacles of Powerhouse Parramatta’s five opening exhibitions – including a tribute to space and flight; a celebration of the shopping mall; a kids’ exhibition themed around the dark; and a showcase of British designer Es Devlin – which otherwise risk sensory overload.

Coups de théâtre abound: secret doorways and dramatic reveals; a mirror maze; a copse of Christmas firs; a massive replica meteorite taking up an entire exhibition space. There’s a recreation of the historic Roselands shopping mall fountain; a restored 1920s elevator transporting visitors with access needs between exhibition floors; and a rainbow-hued walk-in installation by American light artist James Turrell at the top of a tower.

blocks.caption: The historic Roselands shopping mall fountain has been recreated for the Mall exhibition.  Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Throughout the spaces, museum objects (more than 1,600 from the 500,000-strong collection, supplemented by around as many loans) jostle with specially commissioned artworks, lavishly designed displays and interactive exhibits. The exhibitions are fuelled by wonder, spectacle and nostalgia – and are hard to resist.
Planes, engines, rockets – and a James Turrell

Task Eternal is Powerhouse Parramatta’s flagship opening exhibition – and the only one that adults will have to pay an entry fee for ($30/$20 concession; 16 and unders get in free). A celebration of flight and space travel, it takes over the museum’s main hall: 2,000 sq metres with 18-metre-high ceilings, bringing together objects from the Powerhouse collection as well as loans, commissions and literary texts – including excerpts from US science fiction author Ted Chiang, whose short story Tower of Babylon inspired the exhibition’s structure, including a zigzagging tower which visitors ascend and descend.

Hero items include delicate sketches by Leonardo da Vinci; a bumarang (boomerang) – an example of ingenious Indigenous aerodynamic design – collected from Burramatta/Parramatta in the early 19th century; a “boilerplate” (or testing model) Apollo command module from the 1960s; and the spacesuit worn by Leonard Nimoy’s Spock in Star Trek.

blocks.caption: A spacesuit from the film Aliens worn by John Hurt’s character is among others featured in Task Eternal. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: Aircraft from different eras, including the ingenious 19th-century flying rigs of Australian aviation pioneer Lawrence Hargrave, take pride of place. There is an entire room full of engines, and lots of rockets too, including a Skylark research rocket deployed at Woomera in the 70s, and a fully functional retro Rocket Playground from the 1960s.

Among the many stunning artworks, the star exhibit – at the top of the tower – is a perception-testing “ganzfeld” installation by US light artist James Turrell, accessible for those who bought a special Turrell-inclusive ticket ($40 for adults, $10 for kids). Eight viewers at a time are invited into a room with curved walls and a shifting cycle of coloured light, which induces the kind of disorientation experienced by pilots in certain altitudes and atmospheres.

Task Eternal is overwhelming in its scope and visual magnificence. It’s also a little discombobulating. Rather than chronology, it is structured around four “acts” exploring not only the history and technology of air and space travel, but our “cultural relationship with the sky” and “the human compulsion to ascend, leave Earth and return”. It zigzags between eras, topics and modes of storytelling; between science, engineering, design and art.

blocks.caption: A massive sculpture by Torlarp Larpjaroensook, inspired by the Voyager 1 space probe. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: It also works hard to shed the western, patriarchal and colonial narratives around space and flight, and to weave in lesser-known histories and perspectives, including First Nations technologies and cosmologies. This doesn’t make for a smooth, coherent journey; though time, attention to wall texts and repeat visits may yield the kind of rich experience it aims for.
A secret playground that’s sure to be a hit

The Mall, a tribute to the social, cultural and design history of shopping centres, was only partially installed a week ahead of opening, but looks to be similarly maximalist. The Dark, the Powerhouse’s exhibition for children aged 4 to 12 set in a massive replica meteorite more than 22m long, will be an absolute hit – and not just because it’s top secret: no photographs are allowed, and visitors will have to bag their smartphones before entering.

blocks.caption: The Mall exhibition pays tribute to the history of shopping centres in Parramatta and beyond. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: We are allowed to describe how it works though: visitors enter via a dark, narrow tunnel followed by a series of glowing chambers, lined and stuffed with more than 800 objects, including sparkling minerals, retro toys, ancient artefacts and modern treasures (including the first item the museum collected, in 1882: a jar of peas). Part playground, part discovery trail, items are arranged from toddler to adult height, and there are enough hidden delights and nostalgic treats to thaw the most frosty heart – including animations drawing on First Nations creation stories, and the museum’s most Googled object: a heart-emblazoned shirt worn by Leonardo DiCaprio in Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet. There’s not much narrative here, and some might grumble that it is light on science and learning, but museums desperately need to attract young audiences – and this might do the trick.

The calmest of the opening exhibits, titled Overflow, is an installation on the eastern building’s third floor: a 16-metre high-definition LED display of short films by director Ivan Sen, featuring breathtaking footage, each spotlighting one of seven Indigenous organisations from NSW who care for water, country and community.

In front of the screen is a shallow pool with water that laps with the tides of the river. Visitors are encouraged to take their shoes off and get their feet wet; there’s a sensorial magic about being 30m high, with your feet in the water and the sky on either side of you.

blocks.caption: Ivan Sen’s films are displayed on a 16-metre screen in an installation that will have water lapping at your feet. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We’re on a flood plain,” says Beau James, director of First Nations for the Powerhouse, gesturing to the Parramatta River out the window. In fact the location of the building was its own controversy for that very reason. “That river has always ebbed and flowed, that’s its natural way of moving. We wanted to honour water.”

As part of the commission, the museum invested an undisclosed amount of money in the organisations featured in Sen’s films. “We asked them: ‘What’s something you’ve always really wanted to do but have never been able to get funds for?’” says James.

The funded proposals include tagging marine life in Gamay (Botany Bay); clearing rubbish and mitigating pollution in the Parramatta River; and an initiative for clearing invasive European carp from the Barwon River in Brewarrina.
Es Devlin’s Australian debut

The final exhibition brings together recent works by British designer Es Devlin whose peripatetic career has encompassed theatre, fashion, public art and arena concerts (she has designed tours for Beyoncé, U2 and Lady Gaga, as well as Olympic ceremonies and Super Bowl half-time shows).

But Powerhouse’s exhibition – her Australian debut – sees Devlin in a more poetic and philosophical mode. Made over the last decade (and adjusted here for their Australian debuts), the five works, spread across four main rooms, represent Devlin’s attempts to use participatory art and interactive design to induce shifts of awareness and perspective; and to help rewire our sense of connection to the living world and each other.

blocks.caption: Es Devlin’s giant mirror maze takes up 24m x 10.7m of floor space. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: The visual highlight is a giant mirror maze, designed to represent the “arterial geometries of lungs and trees”. But the soul of the exhibition is the participatory work Collective Portrait: a room with a 24m table and an equally long, unspooling reel of white paper, with an invitation to sit down on either side of the table for 15 minutes and draw the person opposite you.

The point is not so much the drawing as the silent interpersonal exchange between strangers. “I’ve been practising this around the world, and I’ve found whoever I practise it with, it can be quietly transformational,” says Devlin.

She has also created a sixth, temporary work for the museum’s month-long opening festival: an Australian iteration of her 2022 outdoor work Come Home Again, featuring her own hand-drawn sketches of 244 endangered local species, and choral tributes which will be performed at dusk most nights through November within her illuminated outdoor installation on the Powerhouse’s riverside lawn.

blocks.caption: Es Devlin’s Memory Palace. Photograph: Blake Sharp-Wiggins/The Guardian

blocks.text: “I’m hoping that if we set up the rhythm of these evensong moments over the opening days and weeks, that people will continue to gather here. That it’s like a beacon.”

Devlin, who has exhibited in the world’s top galleries and museums, describes Powerhouse Parramatta as a “magnificent” building with “astounding” opening exhibitions. “The fact that people are going to not just learn things but feel things and therefore remember what they learned? I think it’s going to make it a destination for people to come from far and wide.”

articles.title: [OPINION] Government must outlive administrations
articles.summary: Here’s a proposal: A Government Development Project Continuity Act and a Philippine Economic Development Board

blocks.text: A persistent weakness of Philippine governance is the tendency of successive administrations to treat development programs as political legacies rather than continuing obligations of the state. Projects initiated by one administration are sometimes suspended or abandoned by its successor, not because they have become unviable, but because they are associated with the previous leadership.

This is wasteful and contrary to the public interest. Roads, bridges, hospitals, irrigation systems, and other development projects are not presidential gifts; they are public investments financed by taxpayers, borrowed funds, or assistance secured in the name of the Republic.

The Philippines needs laws and institutions to protect development commitments across political transitions and turn long-term strategies into results. I propose two complementary reforms: a Government Development Project Continuity Act and a Philippine Economic Development Board (PEDB), drawing on the strategic functions of Singapore’s Economic Development Board (EDB).
Major projects take years to plan and implement. Abandonment without compelling justification wastes public money, leaves unfinished structures, and deprives communities of expected benefits.

Abandonment is especially damaging when foreign financing is involved. It can trigger liabilities, forfeit ODA, loans, grants, or technical assistance, and undermine the Philippines’ credibility as a development partner. Agreements made in the Republic’s name should survive changes in political leadership.
Political succession should never become institutional repudiation.

Congress should establish a legally enforceable presumption of continuity for duly approved, funded, and contractually committed national and local development projects. Coverage should include domestically funded, foreign-assisted, and public-private projects.
The law should provide for:

items: Presumption of continuity. A change in administration or political priorities alone should not justify discontinuing a qualified project.

National registry of protected development projects. A public, secure, interoperable registry should record each project’s cost, funding source, implementing agency, contractual obligations, status, and completion date. Blockchain or equivalent tamper-evident technology could authenticate and timestamp entries and amendments without erasing the project’s history, subject to lawful confidentiality restrictions.
Transition reporting. Every incoming administration should inventory inherited projects and report their status, financial commitments, implementation issues, and completion requirements.

Justified discontinuation. Cancellation or substantial modification should require demonstrable grounds, such as corruption, serious technical defects, economic infeasibility, environmental or safety concerns, material changes in circumstances, or a demonstrably superior alternative serving the same purpose.

Independent review and accountability. Major cancellations should undergo technical, financial, and legal assessment. Foreign-assisted projects should involve consultation with development partners, consistent with applicable agreements. Proposed discontinuations should be publicly explained, with their financial and social consequences disclosed. Congress should exercise oversight, and officials who unlawfully circumvent safeguards should face appropriate liability.

blocks.text: The principle is simple: continuity is the rule; discontinuation is the exception that must be justified.

Protection must not be absolute. Future administrations and Congresses retain authority to correct defective projects, respond to changed circumstances, and exercise constitutional control over appropriations. The aim is to prevent arbitrary abandonment, not guarantee funding regardless of merit or fiscal capacity.

Project continuity alone cannot drive economic transformation. The Philippines also needs an institution able to translate long-term priorities into investment, industrial development, and sustained execution.

Singapore’s Economic Development Board, established in 1961, offers an example of an institution that helped attract strategic investment, develop industries, and strengthen technological capabilities. These principles can be adapted to Philippine circumstances.

We already have relevant institutions: the Board of Investments (BOI), Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA), Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA), Clark Development Corporation (CDC), and other investment promotion and economic zone authorities. The problem is fragmented responsibilities and overlapping functions.

Rather than create another coordinating council, Congress should establish the PEDB by consolidating these agencies under one governing authority and executive leadership. It should be an integrated institution, not merely a body coordinating independently directed agencies.

BOI, PEZA, BCDA, SBMA, CDC, and other relevant agencies should become specialized operating divisions or constituent units. The necessary regulatory, administrative, technical, commercial, and operational responsibilities should be preserved. PEZA should retain specialized zone administration; BCDA should retain its property development capabilities; and freeport authorities should continue their geographically specific functions.

The institutional structure within which they operate must change. The principle is unity of command with functional specialization: one national authority, one coherent strategy, and one accountable executive leadership. Overlapping promotion, investor assistance, administration, and reporting should be rationalized without sacrificing expertise or regional capabilities.

The PEDB should attract investment, develop priority industries, administer economic zones and strategic properties through specialized divisions, connect foreign investors with Filipino enterprises, strengthen local supply chains and technology transfer, and facilitate investment. It should maintain the National Register and monitor implementation.

The PEDB needs professional management, merit-based appointments, staggered terms, and legally defined grounds for removal. Its performance should be measured by realized investment, quality jobs, exports, productivity, technology transfer, and stronger domestic industries—not merely investment pledges. It must remain subject to congressional oversight, Commission on Audit examination, transparency, and independent evaluation.

Consolidation must not create a competing national planning authority. DEPDev should remain responsible for national economic planning, the Philippine Development Plan, and public investment programming. PEDB should translate these priorities into investment and industrial development.

DEPDev plans; PEDB mobilizes investment and drives development; DBM handles budget formulation; DOF oversees fiscal policy and public financing; and Congress legislates, appropriates, and exercises oversight.

These reforms require careful drafting and an orderly transition. The PEDB Act must specify which agencies are merged, which become operating divisions, and which corporate entities or subsidiaries retain separate legal identities. It must address assets, liabilities, contracts, financing, personnel, and ongoing projects; respect vested rights and binding obligations; and amend or harmonize agency charters where necessary. Transitional safeguards must prevent reorganization from disrupting the projects and investments the reforms seek to protect.
Unity of command must be accompanied by clarity of legal authority, continuity of obligations, and accountability for results.

The two reforms are complementary: the Continuity Act protects legitimate commitments from arbitrary disruption; the PEDB consolidates principal investment and development agencies under one authority to drive economic transformation.

Neither should perpetuate defective projects or misguided policies; both require transparency, fiscal discipline, evaluation, and accountability. But a change in administration should not automatically change the country’s economic direction.

National development is cumulative. Every administration should build on what its predecessor accomplished, not start from scratch each time. Measure leadership by its contribution to the country’s continuing progress, not by how effectively it erases previous accomplishments.

Presidents come and go. Administrations rise and fall. But the state endures, and its responsibility to the Filipino people must endure with it. National development must outlive political administrations. It is time to make that principle the law of the land. – Rappler.com

Raul F. Borjal is a BS Economics alumnus of Ateneo de Manila University and has undertaken post-graduate studies at the Ateneo Graduate School of Business. He held senior executive positions in various domestic and multinational corporations, culminating in his retirement as vice president and corporate secretary of a Filipino-owned group of companies.

One of two people charged in relation to the death of an 11-year-old Burnaby, B.C., boy appeared in a Vancouver courtroom for the first time on Thursday.
Branko Bijelic, 51, is charged with second-degree murder and indignity to human remains in the death of Kai Pavlovic.

He sat quietly during proceedings, which were put over until later this month.

articles.title: Ex-DDS cop's testimony sought by ICC prosecutors vs. Rodrigo Duterte
articles.summary: THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors ask judges to admit preserved testimony from an alleged former member of the Davao Death Squad (DDS), whose evidence they say…
articles.byline: Andy Peñafuerte III, Jay-vee Marasigan Pangan

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 6:34am

THE HAGUE, Netherlands — International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors ask judges to admit preserved testimony from an alleged former member of the Davao Death Squad (DDS), whose evidence they say bears directly on former President Rodrigo Duterte’s alleged criminal responsibility.

In a redacted filing made public dated November 5, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang asked Trial Chamber III to admit 45 transcribed statements and 61 items of associated materials from witness P-0002, identified as a former Davao City police officer.
Those supporting items include P-0002’s handwritten notes, affidavits, photographs, four organizational charts of the DDS structure, police service records, and other personal and official documents.
Unlike recent applications made by the Office of the Prosecutor under Rule 68, this request seeks admission of P-0002’s evidence under Article 69(4) of the Rome Statute.

That article states that the court “may rule on the relevance or admissibility of any evidence” considering its probative value as well as “any prejudice that it may cause to a fair trial or to a fair evaluation of the testimony of a witness.”
DDS structure, alleged policy

Prosecutors described P-0002’s evidence as being “of particular importance” to Duterte’s case, as the witness was a member of the Davao Death Squad. However, the period of his alleged membership is redacted.
His testimony covers Duterte’s alleged individual criminal responsibility and intent, the contextual elements of crimes against humanity during Duterte’s mayoral period, and charged Incident 1.

In the Prosecution’s Trial Brief, Incident 1 refers to the killing of three unidentified alleged drug pushers by DDS members in or around 2013 in San Rafael, Davao City. In this incident, then Davao City Mayor Duterte “instructed police DDS members that there was a job to be done against three alleged drug pushers”.

Prosecutors said P-0002 provided evidence on the origins, structure, and purpose of the DDS, as well as the scope of what the prosecution calls the “Common Plan” in Davao City and the roles of alleged co-perpetrators.
His testimony also concerns the alleged widespread nature of the killings, the targeting of suspected criminals, and the DDS’s alleged modus operandi during the charged period.

According to prosecutors, P-0002’s evidence supports the alleged existence of a policy to “neutralise” suspected criminals in Davao City through measures that included financial incentives, the use of state and civilian forces, and the dissemination of the policy by Duterte to alleged perpetrators.
“Unique opportunity”
Prosecutors interviewed P-0002 from May 10 to 16, 2022, after Pre-Trial Chamber I authorized the interview amid concerns that his evidence might later become unavailable.
The Chamber found a “unique opportunity” to interview P-0002 and a significant risk that his evidence “may not be subsequently available.”
A defense counsel appointed to protect the interests of any future accused was present during the interview, along with counsel for P-0002.

The filing says prosecutors were informed of a development concerning P-0002 in June 2024, but the details are redacted. It later states that “P-0002 is no longer available,” but does not expound or clarify.
Prosecutors argued that the preserved testimony should be admitted under Article 69 because it was obtained through a judicially authorized evidence-preservation procedure.

They said it could alternatively be admitted under Rule 68(2)(c) of the ICC Rules of Procedure – or about prior recorded testimony from “a person who has subsequently died, must be presumed dead, or is, due to obstacles that cannot be overcome with reasonable diligence, unavailable to testify orally.”
Trial Chamber III has yet to rule on the request.
Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed during his terms as Davao City mayor and Philippine president.
His trial is scheduled to begin on November 30. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Fox News suffers ratings slump on bleak election night for Republicans
articles.summary: In early, preliminary figures, the news channel trailed several other networks in prime-time viewership

blocks.text: On a midterm election night that was a huge disappointment for Republicans, with Democrats taking control of the US House and Senate, the country’s most prominent conservative television network seemingly felt the brunt of viewer disillusionment with Donald Trump and his party, according to final audience numbers released on Thursday.

The Fox News Channel, which often leads among all news networks in viewership on election nights, fell behind two top broadcasters on Tuesday. According to ratings dating from the Nielsen firm, the network averaged 4.3 million total viewers between 8 and 11pm, behind broadcast networks NBC (6.7 million viewers) and ABC (5.2 million viewers), though it edged out fellow cable networks CNN (4.1 million viewers) and MS Now (3.7 million viewers). Fox News handedly defeat CBS News, which attracted just 2.8 million viewers. CNN performed better in the 25-to-54 age demographic prized by advertisers, besting Fox News, MS Now and CBS.
Originally, preliminary viewership numbers released Wednesday put Fox News behind both CNN and MS Now in total viewership in primetime.

Overall, the big six television networks averaged nearly 27 million total viewers during prime-time election coverage, up from 22.215 million total viewers in 2022. During those 2022 elections, Fox News averaged 7.422 million viewers, meaning its viewership slipped about 41% on Tuesday.

With Trump reaching historic levels of unpopularity, Fox News has seen some viewers tune out in recent weeks. Last month, the network’s viewership was down 27% compared with the same month last year in total day viewers, though it still handily defeated CNN and MS Now. Lachlan Murdoch, the chief executive of parent company Fox Corp, acknowledged “viewer fatigue” in an earnings call on Monday.

Trump, who criticized Fox throughout election night and blamed the network for his party’s losses, poked fun at the network’s October figures in a Truth Social post, chalking up the decline to the channel’s industry-standard practice of booking Democratic candidates for interviews.

“FoxNews Ratings are way down (27%!) because they’re spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats!” he wrote on Tuesday evening. “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me – My numbers are better than they have ever been.”
This story was updated on Thursday afternoon to reflect final viewership figures released by Nielsen.

articles.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk completes second spacewalk, more than six hours long
articles.summary: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is safely back inside the International Space Station after successfully completing his second spacewalk in two weeks.

image.caption: In this screenshot of a NASA livestream, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk performs his second ever spacewalk outside the International Space Station. (NASA)

blocks.text: Science·New
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is safely back inside the International Space Station after successfully completing his second spacewalk in two weeks.
Kutryk stepped out into space with NASA astronaut Anil Menon to work on installing a solar array
Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon stepped into the vacuum of space Thursday morning after undergoing lengthy and detailed preparations with the help of their support team.
Kutryk was first to emerge from the Quest airlock, with a red stripe on the legs of his spacesuit setting him apart from his colleague.

It was the second spacewalk for Kutryk, who became the fifth Canadian to perform the feat on Oct. 29 when he and Menon worked together to install new solar arrays needed to upgrade the station's power capacity.
It was the fifth spacewalk for Menon, NASA said.
This latest spacewalk came in just shy of seven hours, officially lasting six hours and 59 minutes before crew members made their way back inside the space station.
NASA astronaut Anil Menon performs work on the outside of the International Space Station on Thursday. (NASA)
The astronauts were working to install the eighth and final solar array on the starboard side of the truss, which serves as the station's structural backbone.
Video of the spacewalk broadcast by NASA showed the two working step by step with tools Thursday morning while tethered to the space station, sometimes with Earth in the background.
Spacewalks dangerous but necessary
The Canadian Space Agency says spacewalks are among the most difficult and dangerous tasks for astronauts but are needed to repair or install equipment or carry out manual work.

items: A spacewalk to remember: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says seeing Earth 'changed' him
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk conducts his 1st spacewalk

blocks.text: The campaign to upgrade the solar arrays began in 2021 and is expected to increase the station's power-generation capacity by up to 30 per cent, according to the agency.
Before Kutryk, the last Canadian to perform a spacewalk was David Saint-Jacques in 2019.
Joshua Kutryk's 1st spacewalk just part of Canada's huge day in space
Kutryk and his fellow crew members took off for the International Space Station on Oct. 1 for a mission expected to last six months.

The Canadian Space Agency said several Canadians played key roles in Thursday's spacewalk. Those include CSA astronaut Jenni Gibbons, who communicated with the crew as capsule communicator, or CAPCOM, from Houston.
The Canadarm2 robotic arm was used to move the solar array, while CSA teams in Longueuil, Que., helped support operations.
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is shown at the Kennedy Space Center on Merritt Island, Florida in March 2026. (Kelly Malone/The Canadian Press)
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Rush announces week-long concert series in Las Vegas
articles.summary: Rush may be currently delighting fans while on tour, but the Canadian Music Hall of Famers are already prepping for the next high-profile gig soon after its wraps: a week-long residency at immersive…

image.caption: On the heels of their current, much-lauded tour, iconic prog-rockers Rush will dive straight into another high-profile gig: a week-long residency at immersive Las Vegas venue Sphere next year. (Chris Young/Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Rush may be currently delighting fans while on tour, but the Canadian Music Hall of Famers are already prepping for the next high-profile gig soon after its wraps: a week-long residency at immersive Las Vegas venue Sphere.
Rock icons vow to 'concoct some new madness' for shows 'to please our fans both visually and viscerally'

Iconic prog-rockers Rush may be currently delighting fans on a much lauded international tour, but the Canadian Music Hall of Famers are already prepping for the next high-profile gig: a week-long residency at the Sphere.
On Thursday, Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson announced the five-concert series, dubbed Elevate from the Norm, set for late May at the immersive Las Vegas venue.
The dates are mere weeks after the scheduled mid-April finale of Rush's Fifty Something Tour, which is taking the reunited band across North and South America, Europe and the U.K.
German drummer Anika Nilles and keyboardist Loren Gold, who have been performing with the Lee and Lifeson, will also join them for the Sphere shows.

Lee revealed that when he first heard about the dome-shaped venue and its wraparound high-tech LED displays, he imagined it a perfect match for "the kind of visual attitude" of Rush's concerts, even though they weren't touring anymore.
"Life is nothing if not surprising and now, here we are, living and touring in the present tense and we are able to make that particular dream come true," he said in a statement.
Rush members honour late drummer Neil Peart at TIFF
Rush's Sphere setlist will include both greatest hits and fan favourites, he said, to celebrate their musical legacy as well as the life of virtuoso drummer and lyricist Neil Peart, who died in 2020.

The band is working to "concoct some new madness to suit this incredible venue," Lee noted, anticipating the chance "to please our fans both visually and viscerally from wherever they might fly in from."
The shows could be just the thing to lure Canadians back to Las Vegas, which has seen visits from Canada — the state of Nevada's largest source of international tourists — plummet.
Las Vegas pulls out all the stops to win back Canadians

Since opening in fall 2023, Sphere has hosted top recording artists and major shows, from opening act U2 to the Backstreet Boys, Phish to No Doubt, with Metallica, The Eagles and John Mayer among the latest set for that spherical stage.
VIP and travel packages for Rush's Elevate from the Norm shows go on sale Friday, while the artist presale begins Nov. 11. General public tickets go on sale starting two days after that.

articles.title: To protect 55 witnesses, prosecutors seek 'special measures' during Duterte's ICC trial
articles.summary: THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- With less than a month before the International Criminal Court"s (ICC) trial of Rodrigo Duterte, prosecutors are asking for “in-court protective and special measures” for 55…
articles.byline: Andy Peñafuerte III, Jay-vee Marasigan Pangan

blocks.text: THE HAGUE, Netherlands — With less than a month before the International Criminal Court’s (ICC) trial of Rodrigo Duterte, prosecutors are asking for “in-court protective and special measures” for 55 witnesses from the Philippines and abroad from various security risks.

Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang’s public redacted filing, dated November 5, requests that Trial Chamber III allow measures ranging from using pseudonyms and face and voice distortion to holding closed or private courtroom sessions or providing psychological support while testifying.

These special measures are intended to either “protect the witness’s (or another person’s) safety, physical and psychological well-being, dignity, and privacy,” or are warranted “in light of the high vulnerability of these witnesses,” or to “minimize the impact of testimony by providing psychological and emotional support to the witnesses.”
In the filing, Niang cited previous ICC trials to establish the need for protective and special measures, but much of the reasoning remains obscured.

It may be recalled that during the final status conference, senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls told Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner that the Office of the Prosecutor would submit its suggestions for in-court protective measures before Friday.
At that session, Korner reminded Nicholls and trial lawyer Edward Jeremy to provide suggestions, citing the need for certainty about concrete deadlines and to address “various ramifications”.
“Objectively justifiable risk”

The prosecution’s request was made under Articles 64 and 68 of the Rome Statute and Rules 87 and 88 of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence that deal with protective and special measures for witnesses appearing before the Court.

During Duterte’s trial, the prosecution said it currently expects to rely on the evidence of around 78 witnesses, including 69 who are expected to face oral examinations or be admitted through Rule 68(3) of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

The request covers six categories of witnesses: those in the Philippines who are (1) insider witnesses, (2) crime-based witnesses, (3) another redacted category of witnesses; (4) witnesses living abroad; (5) witnesses admitted into the ICC Protection Program (ICCPP), and (6) prosecution staff members.

Prosecutors said there is an “objectively justifiable risk” to the witnesses, who have flagged concerns about providing evidence, “with some making their cooperation contingent upon being provided anonymity.”
“The reported experiences of witnesses demonstrate that [REDACTED], witnesses face significant objective risks which require protection.”
Insider witnesses’ evidence: implicating Duterte and Bato

Some of the strongest security concerns the prosecution raised in the filing involved Philippine-based insider witnesses whose evidence concerns alleged extrajudicial killings during Duterte's term as mayor of Davao City and his presidency.
Their evidence also concerns specific charged incidents and, in some cases, those that prosecutors say directly implicate Duterte.

The filing states some insider witnesses may also provide evidence on the implementation of an alleged policy to neutralize people perceived or alleged to be involved in drug-related or other crimes through violence, including murder.

Prosecutors said some of this evidence may also implicate former Philippine National Police chief and current Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa, whom the filing describes as a co-perpetrator wanted by the ICC.

“[Dela Rosa] maintains sufficient influence and support in the Philippines to evade arrest based on an ICC warrant — which has now been public for five months, yet he remains at large,” the filing noted.
“Insider witnesses may further be at risk and the focus of renewed attention because of the unsealing of Dela Rosa’s arrest warrant.”
For some insider witnesses, prosecutors are asking judges to allow pseudonyms, face and voice distortion and limited private sessions.
For another redacted group of highly vulnerable insider witnesses, the prosecution is seeking pseudonyms and closed sessions throughout their testimony.
Other Philippine-based witnesses
The filing stated that the “vast majority” of prosecution witnesses reside in the Philippines.
“Crime-based” witnesses, who are all currently in the Philippines, are among those for whom prosecutors seek protection.
Their expected evidence likewise concerns alleged extrajudicial killings during the mayoral and presidential periods, charged incidents and, in some cases, allegations directly involving Duterte.
Prosecutors are asking for pseudonyms, face and video distortion, and private sessions where necessary for members of this group.

“In-court protective measures for witnesses in this category will ensure that they can give evidence freely without fear for their personal safety and without compromising their security or the security of their family members.”
For another group of witnesses residing in the Philippines whose category is redacted, prosecutors are seeking pseudonyms and closed sessions for their entire testimony.
The filing says these witnesses are considered particularly at risk because their evidence implicates Duterte and because of other circumstances withheld from the public version.
The prosecution said numerous witnesses have expressed concerns about giving evidence, with some making their cooperation conditional on remaining anonymous.
Some testimony may be closed to the public

The prosecution is asking for three broad types of measures: protecting witness identities from the public, holding closed or private sessions for sensitive portions of testimony, and providing psychological support.
The filing says private sessions may be treated as a protective measure under Rule 87 or a special measure under Rule 88, depending on the circumstances.
For some witnesses, prosecutors want pseudonyms along with face and voice distortion.

They said closed or private sessions would generally be requested only for limited portions of testimony when necessary, although the prosecution is asking that several highly vulnerable witnesses give their entire testimony behind closed doors.
Those witnesses living outside the Philippines are also covered by the request for pseudonyms, face and voice distortion, and private sessions when necessary.
Other witnesses included in the same request for protective measures have already been admitted into the ICC’s witness protection program.
The filing says revealing their identities could undermine the protection already afforded to them and potentially expose them and their families to continuing risks.

“[I]f any of [the ICCPP witness] identities were to become known, the whole purpose of their protection which has been afforded to the witnesses would be undermined, and they, together with their families would be at risk for an indefinite period of time. The accused has been given the full identifying details for these and is able, therefore, to deal with their evidence without restriction.”
Prosecution staff witnesses
The prosecution is also seeking protective measures for witnesses P-1439 and P-1440, both prosecution staff members.
P-1439 had previously testified in another ICC proceeding under protective measures, including a pseudonym, face and voice distortion, and private sessions.
For P-1439, prosecutors also cited the court’s Regulation 42(1), arguing that protective measures previously ordered in another ICC proceeding should continue to apply in Duterte’s case.
Prosecutors said P-1439 will be called to testify in Duterte’s case and asked that those existing measures remain in place.
P-1439’s testimony will corroborate the evidence from Rule 68(3) witness P-1161 and Rule 68(2)(b) witness P-1348.
No further information was mentioned about P-1440, as this witness has never been mentioned or referenced in any of the fourteen previous filings for Rule 68(2)(b) or Rule 68(3) applications.
The request remains subject to the approval of Trial Chamber III.
Duterte’s trial is scheduled to begin on November 30 before Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou.
He is facing three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder allegedly committed during his terms as Davao City mayor and Philippine president. — BAP, GMA News

The S&P 500 saw its worst session since Trump shook markets with his 'Liberation Day' tariffs

The S&P 500 fell 4.4 per cent Thursday for its worst drop since U.S. President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his "Liberation Day" tariffs.

Website known for politics, arts and culture coverage announces closure just weeks before anniversary

Salon, one of the early internet’s pioneering publications, is closing after more than…
articles.byline: Auzzy Byrdsell in New York City

blocks.text: Salon, one of the early internet’s pioneering publications, is closing after more than three decades, the outlet announced on Thursday.

“It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website,” Salon said in a statement. “It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.”
The site, which built its reputation from politics, arts and culture coverage, announced its closure just weeks before its anniversary on 20 November.

“The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness,” the statement said.
Founded in San Francisco in 1995, Salon said its output “helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.”

Salon, which moved most editorial staff to New York City in the 2000s, was described as the oldest general interest publication on the internet, according to a piece by the Columbia Journalism Review in 2011.

“We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters,” the Salon statement said.
The publication won a plethora of awards for its work through the 1990s, including 1996’s website of the year from Time magazine and 1997’s best website from BusinessWeek.

“Thirty-one years is a remarkable run,” Salon said. “What matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them.”

articles.title: 15 patients released, 5 still hospitalized following bus crash near Mackenzie, B.C.
articles.summary: WorkSafeBC and RCMP are still investigating what police described as a "chaotic scene" when the shuttle bus went off Highway 39, causing hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie to declare a code…

image.caption: The University Hospital of Northern B.C. in Prince George declared a code orange Wednesday afternoon following a major bus crash that threatened to overwhelm its resources. (Tom Popyk/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

WorkSafeBC and RCMP are still investigating what police described as a "chaotic scene" when the shuttle bus went off Highway 39, causing hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie to declare a code orange.
WorkSafeBC investigating alongside RCMP after 'chaotic' crash
Northern Health says 15 people have been released from hospital and five are still receiving care following a major bus crash near Mackenzie, north of Prince George, B.C., Wednesday.

WorkSafeBC and RCMP are still investigating what police described as a "chaotic scene" when the northbound shuttle bus went off Highway 39, causing hospitals in Prince George and Mackenzie to declare a code orange. No other vehicles were involved.
Six air ambulances and six ground ambulances treated and transported 20 patients with injuries ranging from minor to serious, according to B.C. Emergency Health Services.

Northern Health says all 20 patients were taken to hospital in either Prince George or Mackenzie, with fifteen being treated and released. Four others remain in care locally, while one was airlifted to another facility elsewhere in the province.
About 20 people hospitalized after bus crash near Mackenzie
Updates on their conditions are not being shared by BCEHS, Northern Health or RCMP, who all cited patient privacy.

items: About 20 people injured, several seriously, in northern B.C. bus crash: police

blocks.text: Operations at both hospitals have since returned to normal, with Northern Health thanking "the physicians, nurses, first responders and other health professionals in Mackenzie and Prince George whose rapid and highly-professional response saved lives and prevented this tragic incident from taking an even greater toll on the victims."
'Nothing has been ruled out': Police
B.C. Highway Patrol has taken control of the investigation, with RCMP saying that while no arrests have been made, "the cause of the crash is still uncertain" and "nothing has been ruled out."
WorkSafeBC is also investigating with a spokesperson saying they are "working with law enforcement partners to establish an understanding of the factors related to this incident."
The shuttle bus was carrying workers subcontracted by Iren, a multinational data centre company with facilities in Mackenzie and Prince George.

articles.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says he'll commute all death row sentences to life in prison
articles.summary: California governor Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the…

image.caption: California Governor Gavin Newsom says he will commute the sentences of all 548 death row inmates in California to life in prison. (Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

California governor Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the values of California, undermines the foundations of the legal system and "diminishes each of us."
There are currently 548 people on death row in the state, the highest number in the U.S.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom says he will commute the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no possibility of parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the values of California, undermines the foundations of the legal system and "diminishes each of us."

In an open letter, Newsom says his decision comes after three decades of openly opposing state-sanctioned executions. He issued a moratorium on all inmate executions in the state in 2019, but said it wasn't enough as their death sentences remained intact.
There are currently 548 people on death row in California, which Newsom describes as "the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere."
California last put a ⁠prisoner to death in ⁠2006, when Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger was ‌governor.

Newsom's decision, which he calls the most difficult of his career, comes just months before the end of his eight-year term as governor, and amid speculation he will launch a bid to run as the Democratic candidate for president in 2028.
Newsom speaks with incarcerated men at San Quentin State Prison in San Quentin, Calif., in March 2023. (Eric Risberg/The Associated Press)
Requires state Supreme Court approval

The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court's approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70 per cent, according to numbers provided by Newsom's office.
California voters rejected a ballot measure in 2016 that would have repealed the death penalty in the state.
"I recognize the limits of this clemency action," Newsom wrote, "which does not repeal the death penalty and is limited to commuting California's current death sentences."
Repealing the law rests with the legislature and voters, but he says that, as governor, he has clemency authority "for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice."
"For me," he said, "this is that moment."

Last month, the California District Attorneys Association sent a letter to Newsom expressing "grave concerns" about the possibility he would commute the sentences, warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional anguish on victims' families.

"Every death sentence in California represents an individual case in which a jury heard the evidence, considered the circumstances and determined that the most serious punishment under our law was warranted," association President Jeannine M. Pacioni said.
"To simply erase all those judgments with the stroke of a pen, without considering the facts of each case or the families affected, would be a profound disservice to the administration of justice."
Newsom said he is aware his decision will surface painful memories for the families of victims of crime.
"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," Newsom wrote.
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, seen here in December 2007, survived two state-sanctioned execution attempts in September. (J. Miles Cary/ Knoxville News Sentinel/USA Today Network/Reuters)
Renewed debate over capital punishment

The debate over capital punishment in the U.S. intensified recently after Tennessee's failed execution of condemned killer Christa Pike, ‌who survived two attempts to inject her with lethal drugs on Sept. 30.
Pike was hospitalized afterward and was sent back to prison on Oct. 10.

The death penalty received further scrutiny after U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to ​livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more ⁠than 30 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in ⁠Texas on Nov. 5, 2009.
U.S. President Donald Trump later ruled out a livestream ⁠of ⁠the execution, but Hasan is still ​scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.
LISTEN | The debate over the death penalty:
As It Happens1:14:47A botched lethal injection reignites death penalty debate
ACLU welcomes move
The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded Newsom's announcement.

"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," executive director Anthony Romero said in a statement.
The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California's death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.
Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.

In 2023, Newsom announced plans to transform San Quentin prison, a facility in the San Francisco Bay Area known for maintaining the largest number of prisoners on death row in the country, into a place where inmates could be rehabilitated and receive job training before returning to society.
That work was completed earlier this year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Stephanie Hogan is a digital producer with CBC News, based in Toronto. She writes on a variety of subjects, with an interest in politics, health and the arts. She was previously political editor for The National and worked in various roles in TV and radio news.
With files from The Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Canada's new budget proposes $5B for culture. Here's where it would go
articles.summary: The Carney government's new budget proposes roughly $5 billion over the next five years toward several initiatives to promote Canadian culture, including building new recreational facilities and ice…

image.caption: People arrive in atrium of the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa on Saturday, July 18, 2020. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

The Carney government's new budget proposes roughly $5 billion over the next five years toward several initiatives to promote Canadian culture, including building new recreational facilities and ice rinks, supporting national museums and permanently making their admissions free for people 25 and younger.
New money to support national museums, building recreation facilities, ice rinks
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 05, 2026 4:06 PM EST | Last Updated: 22 minutes ago
That figure includes more funding for CBC/Radio-Canada and the Local Journalism Initiative.

"Being sovereign means building a country where Canadian culture in all its diversity and creativity thrives," the 2026 budget reads, adding Ottawa is "investing in the stores, places and experiences that connect Canadians to their country and to one another."

The budget proposes providing $1.5 billion over nine years through the Build Communities Strong Fund to support the construction, expansion, retrofit and rehabilitation of community recreational facilities and ice rinks across the country.
Budget focused on affordability, opportunity and sovereignty, Carney says

It also intends to provide $783.1 million over five years, starting this year, to support Canada's national museums, the National Battlefields Commission, the National Arts Centre and Library and Archives Canada.

"This investment will help repair and renew aging facilities, protect national collections and sustain the exhibitions, performances and services that connect Canadians to our history and culture," the budget says.
The national museum funding includes $46.3 million over five years for permanent, year-round free admission for children and youth under 25, plus $11.5 million ongoing.
Other notable items include $76 million in 2027-28 to renew the Canada Strong Pass for another summer.
Ottawa launches 'Canada Strong Pass' to promote domestic tourism | Hanomansing Tonight
The pass gives people free entry to all sites operated by Parks Canada, and free or discounted Via Rail trips depending on age.

Ottawa is proposing a $300-million Canada 160 Fund, an initiative to mark the country's 160th anniversary. The fund will support Canada's Heritage Minutes, the Trans Canada Trail and other community spaces.

items: History, war museums to slash dozens of positions
New Canada Strong Pass offers discounts on parks, museums, camping and train travel

blocks.text: It also intends to provide $15.9 million over four years, starting next year, and $2.1 million ongoing to Veterans Affairs Canada to "acquire, remediate and operate" the National Field of Honour military cemetery.
There is a proposal to provide $11.4 million over three years, starting this year, to Veterans Affairs Canada to support the commemoration of defining moments in Canada's military history.
Funding for journalism, media, artists
The budget pitches an additional $300 million over two years, starting this year, to CBC/Radio-Canada to "strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country."

It proposes $134 million over four years, starting next year, and $41 million ongoing to Canadian Heritage for the Local Journalism Initiative, which is meant to help organizations hire or pay journalists in underserved communities.
The federal government also wants to extend the enhanced 35 per cent Canadian Journalism Labour Tax Credit — set to expire next month — to 2028.
TV crew pass a CBC logo at their headquarters in Toronto, on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

Print journalism currently has access to the credit, and Ottawa wants to expand the credit to "qualifying private audio and audiovisual news organizations, in line with support provided to news organizations that produce written news."
The budget says the extended and expanded credit would cost an estimated $501 million over five years, starting this year, and $85 million ongoing.
The budget also proposes to establish a free national digital book collection. The federal government aims to provide $32.2 million over four years, starting next year, to get the collection started.
According to the budget, the digital collection would launch with at least 200 titles in 2027, then grow to more than 2,000 titles with capacity for up to two million loans annually by 2031.

A man walks past a part of the Emily Carr collection titled, "Fresh Seeing a French Modernism and West Coast," on exhibit at the Royal BC Museum in Victoria, B.C., on Oct. 28, 2020. (Chad Hipolito/The Canadian Press)
The federal government says it will consult with Canadians and the cultural sector on a new Canada Creative Credit — which is expected to take the form of a non-refundable personal income tax credit.

The budget says when combined with the basic personal amount every filer has exempted from income tax, artists could have up to $45,000 of annual net business income derived from original and creative works exempted.
Details on the Canada Creative Credit will be announced in the 2027 spring economic update, the budget said.
Money for ocean preservation
The federal government classifies its proposed investments in Canada's oceans under its cultural plan.

To that end, the 2026 budget pitches establishing and operating two additional National Marine Conservation Areas. Ottawa is proposing $282.7 million over 11 years, starting next year, and $18 million ongoing to Parks Canada toward the initiative.

items: Carney announces $1.2B in funding to protect oceans as major projects loom

blocks.text: Plus, the budget proposes $9.2 million to Parks Canada and $10.5 million to Fisheries and Oceans Canada to support feasibility assessments for up to three additional National Marine Conservation Areas in the North.
Both those sums would come over four years, starting next year.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Lopez Steven is an associate producer for CBC's The House and a digital writer with CBC Politics. He was also a 2024 Joan Donaldson Scholar and a graduate of Carleton University. You can reach him at benjamin.steven@cbc.ca or find him on X at @bensteven_s.
